claims.text: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn is initially a single-phase FCC crystal.
The initial crystal contains pre-existing vacancy clusters or solute inhomogeneities.
Yield strength is largely insensitive to strain rate from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
The strain-rate insensitivity arises because dislocation nucleation occurs over local energy barriers at defect sites rather than through time-dependent dislocation-density accumulation.
The proposed local nucleation sites are vacancy clusters or solute clusters.
Vacancy clusters act as local stress concentrators for Shockley-partial nucleation.
Shockley partial dislocations create intrinsic stacking faults without forming HCP phase nuclei.
Yield stress depends on crystal orientation.
The <11-1> orientation has a higher maximum yield stress than the <110> orientation.
The higher yield stress assigned to <11-1> is caused by a higher Schmid factor for Shockley-partial nucleation.
The critical resolved shear stress is determined by local lattice resistance and orientation-dependent Schmid factors.
The observed HCP-like regions are intrinsic stacking faults rather than a true phase transformation.
Intrinsic stacking faults can be identified by characteristic fault vectors such as 1/6<112>.
Absence of long-range lattice-parameter shifts supports identifying HCP-like regions as stacking faults rather than a transformed phase.
A true FCC-to-HCP transformation would produce lattice-parameter changes or long-range symmetry breaking.
Yield strength decreases monotonically with increasing temperature in the relevant temperature range.
The proposed mechanism applies only from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1 and where thermal activation dominates.
The proposed mechanism excludes conditions in which twinning or FCC-to-BCC transformation occurs.

contradictions.description: The phrase 'athermal thermal activation' combines mutually inconsistent descriptions of nucleation, and the mechanism separately labels nucleation as athermal.
The mechanism specifies athermal nucleation, while the boundary says the hypothesis is valid where thermal activation dominates.

The initial-state field asserts pre-existing vacancy clusters or solute inhomogeneities, whereas the uncertainty field states that the nature of the nucleation sites cannot be confirmed from the available evidence.
